items.question: Why do you see TensorLogic as a language with the properties AI needs?
items.object: TensorLogic as a language for AI
items.answer:
Well, TensorLogic in many ways is the goal that I've been working towards my entire professional life because I really do strongly believe that a field cannot take off until it has really found its language. And TensorLogic, I believe, is the first language that really has all the key properties that you need in the language of AI. For example, it has automated reasoning right out of the box, like Prolog has. The classical languages had a number of things that we just took for granted. The transparent and reliable reasoning, you didn't even have to worry about; it was just already available. At the same time, you don't have that in PyTorch at all. You have all these hacks to try and do reasoning on top of it. At the same time, the Lisps and the Prologs, they never had the autodifferentiation, the ability to learn. One of the beauties of the current moment in many ways is that you barely have to look at most papers; people barely talk about the learning because it's already implemented under the hood. So, you want that as well, right? And you want the scalability on GPUs, the other thing that things like PyTorch and TensorFlow and whatnot give you. There was no language before that had all of these, and there's a number of others, but these maybe are some of the key ones.

So, TensorLogic is basically a language which, as the name implies, is a marriage, a very deep unification, not just some superficial combination of the tensor algebra that deep networks are all built out of and the logic programming that symbolic AI is built out of. There's only one construct in TensorLogic, and it's the tensor equation. You can do everything with tensor equations.

items.question: How do you see TensorLogic's potential to serve as a common language for AI?
items.object: TensorLogic as a common language for AI
items.answer:
We know very well in computer science that there's no one programming language that is better for everything. There's just people who think it is. Everybody has their favorite language that they believe is the universal solvent, but it never really is. We know also for fundamental reasons, going back to Shannon and whatnot, that there is no language that is the most pithy for anything you might want to say. Having said that, physics is a good example because calculus is so fundamental. Feynman famously said that he thought in calculus. The thing that I found with TensorLogic is that I don't know how much of AI it's going to be or how much it should be. But what I have found, in many ways to my surprise, is that in some ways TensorLogic is more than just a programming language. It really captures the fundamentals of what you need in AI in a way that going in I didn't even think was possible.

All of tensor algebra can be reduced to this operation which, going back to physics, is called the Einstein summation. Einstein summation was introduced by Einstein when he was working on relativity and got tired of writing summation signs. General relativity is all about tensors. He jokingly called it his great contribution to mathematics. You can do all of deep learning with just einsum. All of the matrix multiplications and tensor products are instances of einsum. In symbolic AI, it's all about rules, and TensorLogic is based on this observation that an einsum and a rule in logic programming are the same thing. They are actually the same thing. The only difference is that one is operating on real numbers and the other one is operating on Booleans, but that's just a different atomic data type.

At this point I look at all different things that I and others have done in AI and I think it would be crazy to not do these things with TensorLogic. There may be other better things coming after, but at this point I would say TensorLogic is probably better for what people are doing across the board. But hey, that's me. I may be a little biased.

items.question: What do you see TensorLogic's abstraction adding beyond Einstein summation in frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX?
items.object: TensorLogic's tensor-equation abstraction
items.answer:
It does several things. First of all, the syntax of Einstein in these languages, there's also this package called I-nots, is incredibly clunky. At a very basic level, TensorLogic is just a much pithier, more compact, easier to write and understand way to write Einsteins. Physics and mathematicians are famous to like to say that a good notation is half the battle. This might not seem like a big deal, but my experience is that you can think better and faster once you have this notation. That funky procedure call with these indices and these arrows and these arguments is a nightmare. The syntax of TensorLogic, especially, you write an Einstein like you would write a rule. There's a tensor on the left-hand side and a join of tensors on the right-hand side.

Another very important aspect, and one that I think could prove decisive, is that people don't use Einstein much because it's not very efficient. Under the hood, it's not as efficient as you'd like. I've done some programming of this, and I wound up not using Einstein because it's so slow and clunky. All of that can be fixed once you have this one abstraction of the tensor equation, and you implement it on CUDA, for example. You can optimize the heck out of it, and Einstein will finally be able to reach its potential.

Actually, none of these things should be the most important part. The most important part is that Einstein as we know it is only good for tensor algebra. TensorLogic is a language where the same construct does all the symbolic and all the numeric part, and any mix and variation between them, including learning the symbolic part. These are all things that in Einstein world just didn't exist. People who knew Einstein, whether in AI or mathematics or physics, had no idea that any of this had anything to do with reasoning.

items.question: Where do you see the main conceptual contribution of TensorLogic's tensor joins and tensor projections?
items.object: TensorLogic's tensor joins and tensor projections
items.answer:
To be precise, what I did in the paper is, if you look at the simplest form of logic programming, it's Datalog, the foundation of databases. Most SQL queries are variations on Datalog rules, and Datalog rules are composed of two things: joins and projections. This is like databases 101. I have generalized join and projection to numeric values. There's this thing which I define called the tensor join and the tensor projection, which, when the tensors are Boolean, becomes the regular symbolic database one, but now the numeric version has all these things as special cases. It's also more general than the Einstein.

An OR is by having more rules with the same head. If I have A if B, C and A if D, E, then that means A if B, C or D, E. You could also just put them all in the same equation, because it might be more convenient to say AB plus CD. Doing an OR is a completely straightforward thing, but it's really not where the main action is. It's in the tensor joins and tensor projections.

items.question: How do you think about TensorLogic's suitability as a programming language for AI?
items.object: TensorLogic as a programming language for AI
items.answer: The point is there's two things that you want the language to be. First of all, you want it to be universal, so you can do everything. For AI, surely you want a universal language. You want something Turing complete and Turing large, and TensorLogic is that. But then this is actually the most important and most difficult part: you want something that is at the right level of abstraction for the things that you want to do. NAND definitely is not. I can show with a lot of examples in the paper. For example, you can code a transformer in a dozen tensor equations as opposed to a vast mass of code. When people have a language that suits their needs, then they just get used to that. They often wind up using it even for things that it wasn't the perfect thing for, but at that point it's what they're comfortable with. My guess is that at the end of the day people are just going to do everything in TensorLogic. They know in the back of their heads that yes, there are ORs going on here, and you can think of them as ORs, but they just think of them as joins and projects and tensor equations.

items.question: How do you see TensorLogic answering the agenda you laid out in The Master Algorithm?
items.object: TensorLogic as an answer to the unification agenda in The Master Algorithm
items.answer:
In a way, The Master Algorithm was laying out my agenda, asking the question, “What is the master algorithm?” I did say at the outset, I'm not going to give you the master algorithm in this book. I'm just going to tell you where we are and why I think this is the central goal of AI. I would say that TensorLogic is that answer. In TensorLogic, we haven't talked about that yet, but TensorLogic unifies not just symbolic AI and deep learning, it also unifies things like kernel machines and graphical models.

The factors that graphical models are made of are just tensors. Marginalization and pointwise products, which are what probabilistic inference is made of, are just tensor joins and projections on those tensors that represent potentials and, in the case of Bayesian networks, conditional distributions. At this point, we do have this very simple language where you can do the entire gamut of AI, which honestly I didn't think was going to be possible going in. I thought the answer would be much more complicated.

items.object: TensorLogic's role in constructing a master algorithm
items.answer: TensorLogic per se is not the master algorithm because it's just a language. I would say that it's the scaffolding on top of which you can build a master algorithm. TensorLogic is not just a language, it's also the learning and reasoning facilities under the hood. One of the best things about TensorLogic is that the autograd is incredibly simple. Because there's just one construct, the tensor equation, the gradient of a TensorLogic program is just another TensorLogic program. The learning and reasoning are all there. This is not the master algorithm per se, but it's what we need to produce it, and I intend to produce it on short order.

items.question: How do you see TensorLogic addressing the problem of discovering new structures and representations from data?
items.object: Structure learning and predicate invention in TensorLogic
items.answer:
I actually go into that in the paper, but briefly. The paper is just an informal introduction to these ideas. Inductive Logic Programming is the field that deals with discovering rules from data. But it does this by things like greedy search or beam search, and it's a very large search space and it's extremely inefficient. That's one of the things that killed it, even though it could do all these things that people know in deep learning are just painfully rediscovering.

In TensorLogic, this is one of the best parts of it: the structure learning falls out of the gradient descent. The gradient descent actually does structure learning. On top of that, this is actually the best part as far as the learning is concerned: there is this thing called predicate invention, which is discovering new predicates, discovering new relations that are not in the data, but that explain it better. In some sense, discovering representation like that is the key problem in AI, the Holy Grail. When you look at the world, you don't see pixels. You don't see photons hitting your retina; you see objects. The objects are invented predicates. All the way up to science: Newton's genius was to introduce a new quantity, force, and energy, and entropy, and all these, et cetera.

items.question: Why do you regard TensorLogic as such a powerful architecture for gradient descent?
items.object: Tensor decompositions and TensorLogic as an architecture for gradient descent
items.answer:
Let me give you a hint as to why this is the case. There's this other thing that is folded into TensorLogic, which is tensor decompositions. Tensor decompositions are a generalization of matrix decompositions. A matrix decomposition takes a matrix and decomposes it into two new matrices that together are more compact, but essentially reproduce the same data. There's a generalization of that to tensors called the Tucker decomposition. There's others, but the Tucker one is the most relevant one here.

If you write in TensorLogic a rule schema, including a data tensor on the left-hand side—and your entire data can just be reduced to one tensor—and you write a rule expressing that as a function of a few other tensors, the gradient descent, just as in matrix factorization, will discover the best values for those. If you want to discretize it, say, threshold this and make it Boolean again, you will see what is the concept that it learned, or you can leave it in numeric form. The learning is extraordinarily powerful. I've always thought, and I think a lot of people in deep learning really believe this, that gradient descent can do amazing things provided you give it the right architecture to operate on. In a way, what all these million papers are about is finding the right architecture for gradient descent to operate on. Transformers are a great leap forward, but I think TensorLogic is an even greater leap forward.

items.question: How do you understand TensorLogic's ability to learn network structure through weight learning?
items.object: Structure discovery in TensorLogic
items.answer:
TensorLogic does allow that. You can encode a much more general structure. From the point of view of structure discovery, if you create one of these very general equations that you can in TensorLogic, that in some sense can represent a very broad class of architectures, then what the learning does is it discovers the architecture within that space.

A multi-layer perceptron can be compared with a set of rules. There was a system called KBANN in the early days that did this very cleverly. It initialized a multi-layer perceptron with a set of rules because each neuron is a rule. It's also more flexible because now you can have weights. A single neuron can represent a conjunction and therefore a layer can represent a disjunction and so forth. When you're learning weights in an ordinary neural network, you can actually see it as learning the structure of a set of rules. TensorLogic is doing this at a more powerful level. That was just propositional, and now this is at the full level of generality of first-order logic. You can learn the structure, and then there's more than one way to do that. You can also decide how black and white you want the structure to be, what you want to leave as weights, what you want to discretize. The structure itself can be learned by taking a tensor equation. A tensor equation is a very general thing. When you learn the weights of those tensors, that materializes to a specific network structure.

items.question: How do you see TensorLogic helping researchers choose and refine neural network architectures?
items.object: TensorLogic for choosing and refining neural network architectures
items.answer:
You can also do an entire ConvNet in just one tensor equation. The quintessential example of “complete connections don't work” is a multi-layer perceptron for vision, which you replace with a ConvNet that actually has the local structure. That is also a TensorLogic equation. Now, you're saying, “How do you choose between the ConvNet and then an MLP?” Very good question. There are a range of things you can do. These days, you can start out with a very general structure because GPUs and large server farms are an amazing amount of power for something like this. You can almost brute force that search, provided you have the data. I'm not actually recommending you do that.

More interestingly, one of the key benefits of TensorLogic is that you can write down what you believe are properties of the structure. When you program a network in Python, you have to commit: here's the structure. The only thing that happens is the learning of the weights. In TensorLogic, you don't have to do that. You can set up one of these very general structures and then give a bunch of equations that are things that you believe to be true about the structure but do not completely determine it. Those work like priors, and indeed like soft priors. You can turn up the temperature on this or down and say, “You got to obey this equation and that one; sure, you can override.”

In my experience, this is what is important: the gradient descent, instead of starting from a tabula rasa, has this kind of soft knowledge. Most importantly, you the developer, you the AI researcher, get to refine things. Every deep learning researcher or data scientist knows this: you don't do this a priori and then push the button and hope for the best. There's an iterative loop: you set up the structure, then you learn, you get the results, and then you refine the structure. This makes that more efficient, much more, because you just have to write one more equation or modify an existing equation, and the entire stack of what you learn is much more interpretable than it was before.

items.question: How do you think AI should handle computational irreducibility when predicting and acting in the world?
items.object: Computational reducibility and prediction in AI
items.answer:
The computational reducibility problem is that at some level it is true that, although in principle this is all predictable and reducible, in practice it isn't. How do we handle that? Our brains know how to handle this in a way that AI doesn't. You predict, you computationally reduce everything you can to begin with. I've talked with Steve at some length about this, and I'm much more optimistic about how much is reducible than he is. Your overall universe is not reducible, but it's full of these reducible pieces. In a way, evolution is an accumulation of these reducible pieces.

You want machine learning to discover it, and you want inference to exploit it, but then I have no choice but to keep gathering data and using that to inform your predictions. The physics goal of, “I give you the initial conditions and then I just predict,” the Laplace's demon dream, it is a dream. The problem some of the complex systems people have not realized is that we don't have to do that. Ask any engineer, any aerospace engineer using a Kalman filter. What you do is predict just what's needed, or reinforcement learning: you want to have a sense of where you're going, but at every step of time you recalibrate your predictions with the new data that comes in. You only need to predict things well enough to control them, to make them predictable. We humans are always controlling the world to make it more predictable, and this is what robots need to do as well. This is what I'm trying to support with a language like TensorLogic.

items.question: Why do you see TensorLogic as a language for expressing multiple levels of description and representation?
items.object: TensorLogic as a language across levels of description and representation
items.answer:
I am absolutely arguing that TensorLogic is the language to use in all these layers, and let me give you some evidence towards that. Express relativity in TensorLogic. It's tensors and differentials of tensors and whatnot. TensorLogic does that out of the box. Do the same thing with quantum mechanics. Do the same thing with all these others, with all the different pieces of AI that I know.

Why is that possible, and why does TensorLogic do that? Again, I think this gets at a very deep fact about the universe which complex systems people and physicists have suspected as well: the universe has this amazing property, without which it would not be comprehensible, that you can have a lot of complexity at one level that then organizes itself into a new level at which now a different set of laws applies. In a way, what we do with computers is do that by design. But here's the key: what you want is a language in which to express this process, the whole process by which multiple levels get created, by which multiple representations get created, including different representations at the same level.

Going back to Herb Simon, many people, at least in AI, have believed that the essence of human intelligence is your ability to switch between representations as the problem dictates. As long as you pick one representation, you stuck yourself in the box. At that level, TensorLogic is a meta-representation. It's the way to construct representations. A large language model, to take a very salient example, what has that transformer learned when it looks at all that text? A lot of its parts come from that it has looked—it's like, say, Bill Blake says, it has learned these super algorithms. There's all these different pieces and different ways of doing things that it has gathered from different places, and it doesn't choose between them. It's the prompting and the fine-tuning and all that that then pull out the parts that are better for one thing or another.

We absolutely have to do this in AI. I think it also reflects a deeper truth about the universe. I think there are going to be laws of this.

items.question: How do you understand the role of the star T notation in TensorLogic's representation of recurrent neural networks?
items.object: The star T notation in TensorLogic's representation of recurrent neural networks
items.answer:

You always have syntactic sugar because, for example, in an RNN, you want to express X of T plus one. TensorLogic is Turing complete, but I don't have the T plus one. This is a very simple syntactic piece of syntactic sugar to add. Why wouldn't I do that? There's an 80/20 rule of which of these constructs you want to have.

But the star T is actually a completely different thing. The star T is there for computational efficiency purposes. Star T is a hint about how to implement that tensor that saves a ton of memory. You know this notion of a leaky abstraction; all abstractions are leaky, famously in computer science. TensorLogic is no exception. For the most part, when you write TensorLogic, you don't have to worry about what goes on under the hood, but sometimes you want to. This is precisely one of those things.

The idea of the star T is that sometimes I don't want to be computing a new tensor or even just a new vector for every new thing that I do because that would be a waste of memory. Star T is just saying, you have one vector and you reuse it at every iteration. You have the initial X zero and then X one overwrites it. This is a piece of the language. You can do everything without it, but it would be silly not to use it.

items.question: How do you understand computing an infinite sequence, such as the digits of pi, in TensorLogic?

items.question: Why do you see increasing an autoregressive transformer's context size as different from giving a Turing machine more memory?
items.object: The difference between extending an autoregressive transformer's context and extending a Turing machine's memory
items.answer:
I always get this kind of pushback from people. Autoregressive transformers—and I mean classic autoregression, not extended autoregression, not generalized auto, just autoregressive transformers—are not Turing complete. DeepMind admits this and writes a paper showing how you can extend them to become Turing complete. I'll say something like that and somebody will be like, “Oh, yeah, but if I can't do 100-digit multiplication with this context size, all I have to do is just have more context and then I'll be able to do it.”

I keep making the point: here's the crucial difference. A Turing machine is a finite control with an unbounded rewrite memory. Here's the really cool thing about those Turing machines: they can run, churning, and then they say, “Out of memory.” All you have to do is give them more memory and hit continue. You don't have to reprogram them. You don't have to retrain them when you've increased their context size. That's the whole difference: with a neural network, a traditional transformer, if you increase its context size, go back to the training board, you have to retrain it because you've run out of memory.

items.question: Why do you regard TensorLogic's ability to reason in embedding space as the most exciting and important part of your paper?
items.object: Sound and transparent reasoning in embedding space with TensorLogic
items.answer:
I actually say that of all things in that paper, this is the most exciting and important one: you can do sound and transparent reasoning in embedding space with TensorLogic. How come? Why is that possible? Think of kernel machines for a second, and the Gram matrix, the similarity matrix. What is it? You're in feature space, and for every pair of objects IJ, the dot product of their feature representations. If you embed all your objects, we already know who they are. There's a matrix with the embedding vector for every object, whether it's a word or a token or anything else. Now I can do the dot product of the embeddings of two objects. Let's suppose they're all unit vectors to keep things simple. For the moment, let's say you're not even learning the embeddings yet; your embeddings are random. That's already useful for a lot of things, but it's not where the action is.

There's the following very interesting property: the dot product of a vector with itself is one, but the dot product of two random vectors in a high-dimensional space is approximately zero. Your Gram matrix, your similarity matrix, will be approximately the identity matrix. What happens if I have a tensor logical that operates in this way and then has something like a sigmoid nonlinearity? It's going to clean out that noise and it turns into the identity matrix. Now I have all these rules that are just operating in a purely logical mode. They're Boolean tensors going in, meaning relations, and Boolean tensors going out. That way you can do pure deduction in embedding space with these random embedding vectors. That's already something interesting, but now let's say you learn the embeddings, which of course is the whole point.

When you learn the embeddings, what's going to happen by trying to minimize the loss function is that the embedding vectors of objects about which you tend to make the same inferences will get closer. The gradient descent to minimize the loss is going to make their dot product increase. You'll wind up with a similarity matrix that has high values for objects that are quite similar, and low values for objects that are quite dissimilar. In the limit, one on the diagonal, and now if you turn the temperature parameter—the stiffness of the sigmoid—at one extreme, at zero temperature, you have a step function. The similarity matrix is discretized back to zero-one. At the zero-temperature extreme, you have pure deduction.

items.question: How do you distinguish statistical similarity from the analogical reasoning you see in TensorLogic?
items.object: Analogical reasoning and structure mapping in TensorLogic
items.answer:
Kernel machines in some sense are the least powerful type of analogy. It's just, “Oh, here's a similarity,” or nearest neighbor. I have a distance function. That's not really where the action is. The action is in what is called structure mapping. Structure mapping was proposed by Dedre Gentner, where you solve a problem by mapping its structure to the structure of problems that you know. The canonical example is Niels Bohr's model of the atom, which he came up with by an analogy between an atom and the solar system. The nucleus is the sun, the planets are the electrons. It turns out to be a bad analogy, but it was crucial in the development of physics.

There's also this whole subfield of AI called case-based reasoning, where I might help you solve a problem and I don't try to solve it from scratch because I don't need to. That would be a waste. I go to my database of similar cases and find one and then tweak it. Structure mapping is an extraordinarily powerful thing, but it's the combination of similarity and compositionality which kernel machines per se don't have, but TensorLogic does. The point in TensorLogic is that you do have all the power of the kernel machines, but all the compositionality of symbolic AI. Structure mapping just comes out of the box. You don't need to do anything more to have structure mapping and all the power of analogical reasoning that comes with that.

items.question: How do you understand the scope of TensorLogic's guarantee against hallucination at zero temperature?
items.object: TensorLogic's zero-temperature soundness guarantee
items.answer:
Let's make some distinctions. The only claim I'm making here, because it's the only one you can make, is that TensorLogic at zero temperature in this mode will give you the soundness properties that logic has. Soundness in the technical sense of soundness: all that means is that you only reach conclusions that truly logically follow from the premises. You don't say anything about whether the premises are valid or not. If the premises were hallucinated, so will the conclusions be. There's no magic there, but that is a very important property to have.

If I give a transformer a bunch of true facts, it still hallucinates. That's what I can guarantee will not happen in TensorLogic. Coming up with the true facts, well, that's a different part of the game. You can write them down, you can learn them, you can refine them. You never know for sure if you have the perfect model. Of course, that's more the machine learning and knowledge acquisition part. I think I have a very important guarantee here of non-hallucination, but it's not a guarantee that the model that you're working on came from the real world. That's a whole other neck of the woods.

There's this irony in computer science or in the information technology industry: it moves faster than anything else, but at the same time things never die. You can't kill COBOL.

items.question: Why do you think TensorLogic could overcome the adoption barriers that held back earlier AI languages?
items.object: TensorLogic adoption amid AI's growing importance
items.answer:
The point I'm trying to make is we are precisely at a very relevant moment. Why did languages like Lisp and Prolog fall out? Because they were better for AI than Fortran or C or whatever, or Java. They were niche languages, and the network effects of the more widely used languages and all their aspects completely overrode that. We understand that very well now; people didn't in the '80s. But now we're in a different ballgame. The big technology, the center of everything, is AI. If you have a better language for AI, that is the one that is going to have the biggest users.

Moreover, to adopt a new language or a new anything, like a new app, it needs to solve some big pain. Is there a big pain that TensorLogic solves? Hell yeah. It potentially solves hallucination. It solves opacity. We're in this world right now where there are multi-billion corporations and systems that are driven by this black box. I've talked with CEOs of big tech companies who say, “I can't sleep at night because I don't know what this thing is going to do, and the people who trained it have left the company, and who knows?” If we can make a dent in that, people will convert to it very quickly. Also, when people have the experience of how easy it is to use TensorLogic compared to the big pile of stuff that lies under PyTorch and whatnot, I think they'll be very motivated to migrate quickly.

items.question: How do you envision Python developers making the transition to TensorLogic?
items.object: Incremental migration from Python to TensorLogic
items.answer: The transition to TensorLogic from Python doesn't have to happen all at once. You can write a preprocessor into Python. All it does is a one-to-one mapping between the syntax of TensorLogic and einsum. Making things efficient, as we discussed, is another matter, but from the point of view of developer uptake, there's a long history of people doing this with different languages. You have a preprocessor that lets you write tensor equations, but then it converts those equations into PyTorch or Python or just NumPy, let's say Python. Then you do everything else in Python that you did before. You don't lose any existing code. A set of things, and in particular reasoning, have now become much easier than they were before. Then you have this little lollipop: “Oh, but I can do this, and let me have that piece of syntactic sugar.” Before you know it, people are like, “Well, I don't need all that Python stuff anymore. I'd rather live in TensorLogic world.”

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between declarative and procedural semantics in TensorLogic?
items.object: TensorLogic's declarative and procedural semantics
items.answer: TensorLogic, like Prolog and Datalog, has both declarative and procedural semantics. You can look at a tensor equation. That's the whole beauty of logic programming in some sense: you can look at a TensorLogic equation as an equation. It's like Einstein's equation. It's a statement about the world. But you can also treat it as a function call. The left-hand side is the call, and the right-hand side is the body, which is a bunch of other calls and the way to combine them. In fact, most of the time, in my experience that I've used TensorLogic so far, I tend to use it in procedural mode. It's a set of equations, a bunch of statements, like you would have in any imperative language.

items.question: What value do you see in using TensorLogic's abstraction to teach AI?
items.object: Abstraction in computer science and AI education
items.answer: When you're teaching people something, this is the tragedy of computer science education. From high school to intro courses to the most advanced things, you want to teach them the beauty of what you can do and the essence of the algorithms, but then the students spend all their time bogged down in all this crap, all these details where you get the semicolon wrong and the program doesn't work anymore, and they hate it. They decide that computer science is not for them, or at best, they waste 10 times more time than they should. Precisely the whole point of having the right abstraction is to avoid that. This is one of the best features of TensorLogic, to do that for AI.

items.question: How do you see TensorLogic accommodating the need for low-level efficiency optimizations?
items.object: TensorLogic's ability to express different levels of computation
items.answer: A lot of the time you need to go beyond that level of abstraction, for efficiency and so on. I would say, and we won't know until TensorLogic is used widely and we see what happens, that TensorLogic is a language that at some level is like C. It's very low-level. The beauty in my mind, again, this gets back to the multiple levels, is that you can use it to say very high-level things. You can also express the lowest-level possible computations. A tensor equation is something that you can map onto a GPU with almost no change and optimize the heck out of it. I've joked with folks at Nvidia that CUDA is a nice moat, but TensorLogic could be the end of that moat.

items.question: How do you see the current moment in AI, given the advances made by transformers?
items.object: The current moment in AI
items.answer: In fact, the paradox of the current moment in AI is that on the one hand, this is super exciting. This is what we've worked all our lives towards. It's like the dream is happening. I used to tell people when I went into grad school that one day machine learning is going to take over the world, and they'd be like, “Uh, what?” And I'm like, “See, it is taking over the world. There, take that.” On a more serious note, transformers are a great leap forward, and anybody who's used a chatbot is like, “Wow, look at the things this can do. This is great.” But at the same time, the sheer amount of wastefulness and stupidity and ignorance going on is just unbelievable.

items.question: What do you think researchers at OpenAI working on reasoning could gain from established AI knowledge?
items.object: OpenAI's approach to reasoning and the motivation for TensorLogic
items.answer: I've talked with people at OpenAI that do the reasoning. Many of them are very good people, so I'm not trying to pick on anybody, but it's like, “Oh, what is reasoning? We need to figure that out.” And then they say a bunch of stuff that is completely wrong. I'm thinking to myself, “Why don't you spend an afternoon reading a couple of chapters of Russell and Norvig and save a hundred billion dollars in wasted compute? Please, just do that.” Part of what I'm trying to do with TensorLogic is make things go in that direction, because the current direction is just too damn painful. And it's not just that it's painful. This is going to end badly.
